paragraphs.text: Li et al. (2016) used exome and candidate panel sequencing to study 2 unrelated children with epileptic encephalopathy. Both carried the same de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the GRIN2D gene, c.1999G-A (V667I). The V667I substitution lies in the M3 transmembrane domain of GluN2D, a region involved in channel gating. Functional studies showed that it was a gain-of-function mutation. It increased glutamate and glycine potency 2-fold and channel open probability 6-fold, reduced receptor sensitivity to endogenous negative modulators such as extracellular protons, and prolonged deactivation after glutamate removal.

paragraphs.text: Tsuchida et al. (2018) used whole-exome sequencing to study 3 unrelated patients with severe developmental delay and intractable epilepsy. Each carried a novel heterozygous missense variant in the GRIN2D gene. The altered residues were highly conserved across vertebrates and among the 4 GluN2 subunits. Structural consideration indicated that all 3 variants probably impair GluN2D function, either by affecting intersubunit interaction or by altering channel gating activity.

paragraphs.text: Li et al. (2016) tested the mutant receptors for sensitivity to FDA-approved NMDA receptor antagonists. Based on these results, both children were given oral memantine, and seizure burden and development improved mildly to moderately. The older proband later developed refractory status epilepticus, which improved dramatically with ketamine and magnesium. The authors suggested that NMDA receptor antagonists may be useful as adjuvant epilepsy therapy in individuals with GRIN2D gain-of-function mutations.

paragraphs.text: Li et al. (2016) studied 2 unrelated children with epileptic encephalopathy and refractory seizures. Using exome and candidate panel sequencing, they found the same de novo heterozygous c.1999G-A transition in the GRIN2D gene in both children, resulting in a val667-to-ile (V667I) substitution in the M3 transmembrane domain. The mutation caused a gain of function. It increased glutamate and glycine potency 2-fold and channel open probability 6-fold, reduced sensitivity to extracellular protons, and prolonged deactivation. In transfected cultured neurons, the mutant caused dendritic swelling and neuronal cell death. Treatment with oral memantine led to mild to moderate improvement in both children.
